explanations.answer: God our Savior and Christ Jesus
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Paul says he's an apostle of Christ Jesus "by the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope" (1 Timothy 1:1). Paul isn't saying he picked the job himself. He says it came by their command, and that's a pretty strong way to open a letter.

Good guess, friend, but Paul doesn't mention Jerusalem here at all. He says his apostleship is "by the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope" (1 Timothy 1:1). When Paul opens a letter, he goes straight to the top. No middle management.

Not this time, friend. Paul doesn't name Peter or any other apostles in this opening. He says it was "by the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope" (1 Timothy 1:1). That's the whole source of his calling, right there in verse 1.

Yes, Ephesus! Paul says he urged Timothy to "stay on at Ephesus" when he left for Macedonia (1 Timothy 1:3). Timothy had a job to do there, and Paul wanted him in place to do it. Staying put can be real work, friend.

Close, friend, since Corinth is a city Paul knew well. But this letter says Ephesus: "you should stay on at Ephesus" (1 Timothy 1:3). Paul had left for Macedonia, and Timothy was to hold down the fort in Ephesus.

Antioch is a real city in Paul's story, but it's not the one here. The verse says Timothy should "stay on at Ephesus" (1 Timothy 1:3). I know, I know, so many cities and only one right answer. Even I need a map sometimes.

That's it, friend. Paul wants Timothy "to instruct certain men not to teach false doctrines" (1 Timothy 1:3). The myths and genealogies come right after that in verse 4. So there's a whole pile of things to stop, and false teaching is the first one named.

Not quite, friend. Nothing in these verses says these men refused to work. Paul says Timothy should instruct them "not to teach false doctrines" (1 Timothy 1:3). The problem Paul names is what they were teaching.

That's a topic Paul covers in other places, but it's not in this passage. Here he says Timothy should instruct certain men "not to teach false doctrines" (1 Timothy 1:3). Different letter, different problem, friend.

Right on the money. Paul says the myths and endless genealogies "promote speculation rather than the stewardship of God's work, which is by faith" (1 Timothy 1:4). Speculation is just guessing that goes around and around. Stewardship of God's work, though, is by faith.

Greed is a real thing, friend, but Paul doesn't use that word here. He says these myths and genealogies "promote speculation rather than the stewardship of God's work, which is by faith" (1 Timothy 1:4). The word is speculation. It means guessing, not grabbing.

Good try, friend, but that's not what the verse says. It says the myths and endless genealogies "promote speculation rather than the stewardship of God's work, which is by faith" (1 Timothy 1:4). Those men may have been busy as can be. Paul's point is about where all that effort goes.

Love is the word, friend. Paul says "The goal of our instruction is the love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith" (1 Timothy 1:5). All that teaching is aiming at love. Not at winning, and not at sounding smart.

I get why you'd pick it, friend, since teaching and knowledge go together like dough and chocolate chips. But Paul says "The goal of our instruction is the love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith" (1 Timothy 1:5). Love is the goal.
Not success, friend. Paul says "The goal of our instruction is the love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith" (1 Timothy 1:5). The goal isn't a trophy. It's love.

Careful, friend, this one flips it around. Paul says the opposite: "They want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying or that which they so confidently assert" (1 Timothy 1:7). They don't understand it. So False was the answer here.

Yes, friend, False. Paul says "They want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying or that which they so confidently assert" (1 Timothy 1:7). They want the title, but they don't understand what they're saying. And they say it with confidence anyway!

explanations.answer: It is good if used rightly
explanations.explanation: You got it, friend. Paul says "the law is good, if one uses it legitimately" (1 Timothy 1:8). The law isn't the problem. The problem is people using it the wrong way.

explanations.answer: It has been done away with
explanations.explanation: That's not what Paul says here, friend. He says "the law is good, if one uses it legitimately" (1 Timothy 1:8). Good is his word for it. The trouble is with those who use it wrongly.

explanations.answer: It is too heavy to carry
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend. Paul never calls the law heavy in this passage. He says "the law is good, if one uses it legitimately" (1 Timothy 1:8). Good, when it's used the right way.

Close, friend, but the verse says the opposite. Paul says "law is not enacted for the righteous, but for the lawless and rebellious" (1 Timothy 1:9). So the answer is False. The law is aimed at the lawless.

That's right, friend. Paul says "law is not enacted for the righteous, but for the lawless and rebellious" (1 Timothy 1:9). So the law isn't aimed at the righteous. It's aimed at the lawless and rebellious, and the list that follows spells out who he means.

explanations.answer: The glorious gospel of the blessed God
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Paul says sound teaching "agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God, with which I have been entrusted" (1 Timothy 1:10-11). That's the measuring stick. Teaching that doesn't line up with the gospel isn't sound.

explanations.answer: The traditions handed down by the elders
explanations.explanation: Not this time, friend. Paul never mentions elders' traditions in these verses. He says sound teaching "agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God" (1 Timothy 1:10-11). The gospel is what the teaching has to match.

explanations.answer: The wisdom of the Greek teachers
explanations.explanation: Good guess for a letter going to Ephesus, friend, but Paul doesn't say that here. He says sound teaching "agrees with the glorious gospel of the blessed God" (1 Timothy 1:10-11). The gospel is the standard, not any teacher's wisdom.

True, friend! Paul says the glorious gospel is the one "with which I have been entrusted" (1 Timothy 1:11). Being handed something that important is a big deal. I know a little about being handed a job when I least expected it.

Not quite, friend, it's True. Paul says the glorious gospel is the one "with which I have been entrusted" (1 Timothy 1:11). He didn't invent it or make it up. It was put into his hands, and he's passing it on in this letter.
